stem: During long-term follow-up, a transplant recipient has persistently elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol on immunosuppression. Which coordination step aligns with standard post-transplant care references?

options.text: Assess lipid profile and treat hyperlipidemia aggressively
Ignore lipid elevations because transplantation prevents cardiovascular disease
Defer all lipid assessment until twenty years post-transplant
Discontinue immunosuppression immediately whenever cholesterol rises

explanation.rationale_correct: Long-term post-transplant care includes assessing lipid profiles and treating hyperlipidemia aggressively, with monitoring of treatment response and medication side effects.

rationale_incorrect.B: Transplant recipients remain at cardiovascular risk and require lipid management.
rationale_incorrect.C: Lipid assessment is part of ongoing care rather than being deferred for decades.
rationale_incorrect.D: Immunosuppression changes require transplant-team guidance rather than abrupt discontinuation by the coordinator alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Long-term care → E. Treat hyperlipidemia aggressively
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Assess lipid profile … Treat hyperlipidemia aggressively

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Long-term care → E.1. (assess lipid profile; treat hyperlipidemia aggressively); PDF p. 321 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Aggressive hyperlipidemia treatment coordination angle distinct from hyperlipidemia lifestyle teaching (cctc-1115) and sirolimus lipid side effects (cctc-3077); anchor verified on Cupples p. 321.

stem: When coordinating long-term post-transplant care for a recipient with new hypertension on cyclosporine, which management principle aligns with standard references?

options.text: Treat hypertension aggressively and monitor blood pressure response to therapy
Ignore blood pressure because immunosuppression prevents hypertension
Hypertension requires no monitoring after the first post-transplant week
All antihypertensive agents are permanently contraindicated after transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Long-term post-transplant care includes treating hypertension aggressively, assessing risk factors, and monitoring blood pressure response and antihypertensive side effects.

rationale_incorrect.B: Hypertension may develop as an immunosuppressant side effect and requires treatment.
rationale_incorrect.C: Blood pressure monitoring continues long term rather than ending after one week.
rationale_incorrect.D: Antihypertensive therapy is used when indicated rather than being universally contraindicated.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Long-term care → F. Treat hypertension aggressively
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Treat hypertension aggressively … Monitor response to antihypertensive therapy

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Long-term care → F. (treat hypertension aggressively; monitor BP response); PDF p. 321 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Aggressive hypertension management angle distinct from hypertension as IS side-effect teaching (cctc-1038) and glucose-control coordination (cctc-3111); anchor verified on Cupples p. 321.

stem: When coordinating long-term malignancy surveillance after transplantation, which screening guidance aligns with standard references?

options.text: Routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines
No cancer screening because immunosuppression prevents malignancy
Screening only once at transplant discharge with no follow-up
Screening deferred until thirty years post-transplant for all recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Cancer-prevention care includes routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines, with more aggressive or frequent screening when individual risk warrants.

rationale_incorrect.B: Immunosuppressed recipients have increased malignancy risk and require screening.
rationale_incorrect.C: Ongoing screening is recommended rather than a single discharge assessment.
rationale_incorrect.D: Screening begins per guideline timelines rather than being deferred for decades.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevention of cancer
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Routine cancer screening per American Cancer Society guidelines

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevention of cancer → 5. (routine cancer screening per ACS guidelines); PDF p. 282 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. ACS routine cancer-screening coordination angle distinct from hepatitis B HCC prevention (cctc-1112) and skin self-examination teaching (cctc-3102); anchor verified on Cupples p. 282.

stem: A coordinator is updating post-transplant malignancy-prevention teaching. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Smoking cessation is recommended as part of cancer prevention.
Routine self-examination of skin is recommended.
Tanning beds are a safe alternative to sun avoidance for transplant recipients.
Broad-brimmed hats and protective clothing are sun precautions for recipients.

explanation.rationale_correct: Cancer-prevention teaching includes smoking cessation, routine skin self-examination, and protective clothing such as broad-brimmed hats. Statement III is false because tanning beds should be avoided.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also true—protective clothing is recommended.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement III is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false because tanning beds are not a safe alternative.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevention of cancer
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Smoking cessation … Routine self-examination of skin … Avoiding tanning beds … Broad-brimmed hats

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevention of cancer → 1.–4.c.i. (smoking cessation, skin self-exam, avoid tanning beds, protective clothing); PDF p. 282 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Malignancy-prevention combo distinct from prior malignancy-prevention combo (cctc-3043) and PTLD combo (cctc-3112); anchor verified on Cupples p. 282.
